subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: What is the mass per cent of oxygen in ethanol?
solution:
Ethanol is \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\), i.e. \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}\).
Molar mass \(= 2(12) + 6(1) + 16 = 46\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
One mole carries one oxygen atom, of mass \(16\,\text{g}\).
Mass per cent of oxygen \(= \dfrac{16}{46} \times 100 = 34.73\%\) (exactly \(15.999/46.069\)).
Matches option D.

subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: The statements for laws of chemical combinations are given below. Mark the statement which is not correct.
optA: Matter can neither be created nor destroyed : Law of conservation of mass
optB: A compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by weight: Law of definite proportions.
optC: When gases combine they do so in a simple ratio be weight: Gay Lussac’s Law
optD: Equal volumes of gases at same temperature and pressure contain same number of molecules: Avogadro’ Law
solution:
Gay Lussac's law of combining volumes states that gases react, and their products form, in a simple ratio of their VOLUMES, all measured at the same temperature and pressure.
Pairing that law with "a simple ratio by weight" therefore misstates it: the simple ratio is one of volumes, never of masses.
The other three pairings are correct as written - conservation of mass, definite proportions and Avogadro's law are each stated properly.
Matches option C.

subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: In an experiment, 24 g of iron oxide on reduction with hydrogen gave 1.68 g of iron. In another experiment 2.9 g of iron oxide gave 2.09 g of iron on reduction. Which law is illustrated from the above data?
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] The printed 24 g of iron oxide implies 7 per cent iron, which is impossible for any iron oxide; the intended figure is 2.4 g. The law illustrated is the same under either reading, so the answer stands.

Find the composition of each sample.
Experiment 2: \(\text{Fe} = 2.09\,\text{g}\) in \(2.9\,\text{g}\) of oxide, so \(72.1\%\) iron and \(\text{O} = 0.81\,\text{g}\).
Experiment 1 as printed: \(\text{Fe} = 1.68\,\text{g}\) in \(24\,\text{g}\) of oxide, so \(7.0\%\) iron.
The two samples do not have the same composition, so the data cannot illustrate constant proportions.
Both samples are built from the same two elements, iron and oxygen, combined in two different mass ratios - which is exactly the situation the law of multiple proportions describes.
Reciprocal proportions would need a third element, and conservation of mass would need a total mass before and after a reaction; neither is supplied.
Matches option B.
reviewNote: Printed defect. The first mass reads 24 g on the page (verified at 14x), which makes that sample 7.0% iron - not an iron oxide at all. With 2.4 g it is 70.0% Fe, i.e. Fe2O3 (69.94% calculated), while experiment 2 at 72.1% Fe is Fe3O4 (72.36% calculated) - two different oxides of the same two elements, which is the multiple-proportions pair the question is built on. The LAW identified is the same under either reading, so the key is unaffected; only the arithmetic in the stem is broken. ADJUDICATED 2026-09-12 (dual-blind crosstab conflict, the only one in 150 rows). Pass 1 keyed multiple proportions, pass 2 keyed constant proportions. Settled on multiple proportions from the data: with the intended 2.4 g, sample 1 gives an O:Fe mole ratio of exactly 1.5000, i.e. Fe2O3, while sample 2 gives 1.3565, i.e. approximately Fe3O4. Two different oxides of the same two elements is precisely the law of multiple proportions. Constant proportions is excluded because it would require the two iron percentages to be EQUAL and they are 70.0 per cent and 72.07 per cent. The printed 24 g is a source typo for 2.4 g (24 g implies 7 per cent iron, impossible for any iron oxide), but the law illustrated is the same under the intended reading.

subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: Which of the following pairs illustrates the law of multiple proportions?
solution:
The law of multiple proportions applies when the SAME two elements combine in more than one ratio to form different compounds.
Lead and oxygen give both \(\text{PbO}\) and \(\text{PbO}_2\): for a fixed mass of lead the masses of oxygen stand in the ratio \(1 : 2\).
\(\text{PH}_3\) and \(\text{HCl}\) share only hydrogen, \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) and \(\text{SO}_2\) share only sulphur, and \(\text{CuCl}_2\) and \(\text{CuSO}_4\) share only copper, so no other pair is built from one common pair of elements.
Matches option B.

subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: Which of the following statements best explains the law of conservation of mass?
optA: 100 g of water is heated to give steam.
optB: A sample of \(\text{N}_2\) gas is heated at constant pressure without any change in mass.
optC: 36 g of carbon combines with 32 g of oxygen to form 68 g of \(\text{Co}_2\).
optD: 10 g of carbon is heated in vacuum without any change in mass.
solution:
The law of conservation of mass needs a chemical change in which the total mass before equals the total mass after.
Heating water to steam, heating nitrogen at constant pressure and heating carbon in vacuum are not chemical reactions between two substances, so none of them tests the law.
Carbon combining with oxygen is a chemical change, and the masses balance: \(36 + 32 = 68\,\text{g}\), so nothing has been created or destroyed.
Matches option C.
reviewNote: The chosen option is the only one describing a chemical reaction with a mass balance, and the balance it asserts (36 + 32 = 68) is arithmetically right, so the key is secure. It is chemically loose, though: 36 g of carbon is 3 mol while 32 g of oxygen is 1 mol, so only 12 g of the carbon is consumed and the 68 g of product is 44 g of CO2 plus 24 g of unreacted carbon, not 68 g of CO2. The printed formula in that option also reads Co2 (cobalt casing) for CO2, already recorded in the transcription note.

stem: What quantity of copper oxide will react with 2.80 L of hydrogen at NTP?
solution:
\(\text{CuO} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{Cu} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), so CuO and \(\text{H}_2\) react \(1 : 1\).
Moles of \(\text{H}_2 = \dfrac{2.80}{22.4} = 0.125\,\text{mol}\).
Moles of CuO required \(= 0.125\,\text{mol}\).
Molar mass of CuO \(= 63.5 + 16 = 79.5\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Mass \(= 0.125 \times 79.5 = 9.94\,\text{g} \approx 9.9\,\text{g}\).
Matches option C.

stem: At NTP, 1 L of \(\text{O}_2\) reacts with 3 L of carbon monoxide. What will be the volume of CO and \(\text{CO}_2\) after the reaction?
solution:
\(2\text{CO} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2\); by Gay Lussac's law the volumes react in the same ratio as the coefficients.
\(1\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) consumes \(2\,\text{L}\) of CO and produces \(2\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\).
CO supplied \(= 3\,\text{L}\) and CO used \(= 2\,\text{L}\), so \(1\,\text{L}\) of CO is left unreacted.
After the reaction there are \(2\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(1\,\text{L}\) of CO.
Matches option D.

subtopic: Laws of Chemical Combination and Percentage Composition
stem: Given below are few statements. Mark the statement which in not correct.
optA: Gram atomic mass of an element may be defined as the mass of Avogadro’s number of atoms.
optB: The molecular mass of a diatomic elementary gas is twice its atomic mass.
optC: Gay Lussac’s law of chemical combination is valid for all substances.
optD: A pure compound has always a fixed proportion of masses of its constituents.
solution:
Gay Lussac's law of combining volumes is stated for gases alone, because only gases have the equal-molar-volume property that lets a volume ratio equal a mole ratio; it says nothing about solids or liquids.
Claiming it is valid for all substances is therefore the incorrect statement.
The other three are sound: a gram atomic mass is the mass of \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms, a diatomic element has molecular mass twice its atomic mass, and a pure compound has a fixed mass proportion of its constituents.
Matches option C.

stem: A balanced equation for combustion of methane is given below: \(\text{CH}_{4(g)} + 2\text{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \text{CO}_{2(g)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}_{(g)}\) Which of the following statements is not correct on the basis of the above chemical equation?
optA: One mole of \(\text{CH}_4\) reacts with 2 moles of oxygen of give one mole of \(\text{CO}_2\) and 2 moles of water
optB: One molecule of \(\text{CH}_4\) reacts with 2 molecules of oxygen to give one molecule of \(\text{CO}_2\) and 2 molecules of water.
optC: \(22.4\,\text{L}\) of methane reacts with \(44.8\,\text{L}\) of oxygen to give \(44.8\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(22.4\,\text{L}\) of water.
optD: 16 g of methane reacts with 64 g of \(\text{O}_2\) to give 44 g of \(\text{CO}_2\) and 36 g of water.
solution:
For gases the coefficients give the volume ratio, so \(\text{CH}_4 : \text{O}_2 : \text{CO}_2 : \text{H}_2\text{O} = 1 : 2 : 1 : 2\).
Hence \(22.4\,\text{L}\) of methane needs \(44.8\,\text{L}\) of oxygen and yields \(22.4\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(44.8\,\text{L}\) of water vapour.
The statement offering \(44.8\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(22.4\,\text{L}\) of water has these two products interchanged, so it is the one that is not correct.
The mole and molecule statements follow the coefficients directly, and the mass statement balances: \(16 + 64 = 80 = 44 + 36\).
Matches option C.

subtopic: SI Units, Physical Properties and Atomic Abundance
stem: The reference standard used for defining atomic mass is
solution:
Since 1961 the atomic mass unit has been defined so that one atom of the carbon-12 isotope has a mass of exactly \(12\,\text{u}\); every other atomic mass is measured relative to it.
Matches option B.

subtopic: SI Units, Physical Properties and Atomic Abundance
stem: For every one \(^{37}\text{Cl}\) isotope there are three \(^{35}\text{Cl}\) isotopes in a sample of chlorine. What will be the average atomic mass of chlorine?
solution:
Take the stated ratio as 1 atom of \(^{37}\text{Cl}\) to 3 atoms of \(^{35}\text{Cl}\), i.e. 4 atoms in all.
Average atomic mass \(= \dfrac{1(37) + 3(35)}{4} = \dfrac{37 + 105}{4} = \dfrac{142}{4} = 35.5\).
Matches option C.

subtopic: SI Units, Physical Properties and Atomic Abundance
stem: Atomic masses of elements are usually fractional because.
optB: They contain impurities of other atoms.
optD: Atomic masses cannot be weighed accurately.
solution:
Most elements occur as a mixture of isotopes of different mass number, and the tabulated atomic mass is the weighted average over that mixture, which is generally not a whole number.
Chlorine averages \(35.5\) from its 35 and 37 isotopes in a \(3 : 1\) ratio.
Isobars are different elements sharing a mass number, so they are not present in a sample of a single element, and neither impurity nor weighing error is the reason.
Matches option A.

stem: Which of the following statements about the molecular mass is correct?
optA: Molecular formula shows the exact number of different types of atoms present in a molecule.
optB: Molecular formula can be obtained from empirical formula if molar mass is known.
optC: Percentage composition of a compound can be calculated from its molecular formula.
solution:
A molecular formula does give the actual number of atoms of each kind in one molecule.
It is also obtainable from the empirical formula once the molar mass is known, through \(n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}\).
And percentage composition follows from the molecular formula by dividing each element's total mass by the molar mass.
All three statements are therefore correct.
Matches option D.

stem: The density of a gas is \(1.78\,\text{g}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) at STP. The weight of one mole of gas is.
solution:
At STP one mole of any gas occupies \(22.4\,\text{L}\).
Mass of one mole \(= \text{density} \times \text{molar volume} = 1.78 \times 22.4 = 39.9\,\text{g}\).
Matches option A.

stem: How many number of molecules and atoms respectively are present in 2.8 litres of a diatomic gas at STP?
solution:
Moles of gas \(= \dfrac{2.8}{22.4} = 0.125\,\text{mol}\).
Number of molecules \(= 0.125 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 7.53 \times 10^{22} \approx 7.5 \times 10^{22}\).
The gas is diatomic, so atoms \(= 2 \times 7.53 \times 10^{22} = 1.5 \times 10^{23} = 15 \times 10^{22}\).
Matches option C.

stem: Total number of atoms present in 34 g of \(\text{NH}_3\) is
solution:
Molar mass of \(\text{NH}_3 = 14 + 3 = 17\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), so \(34\,\text{g}\) is \(2\,\text{mol}\).
Each molecule holds \(1 + 3 = 4\) atoms.
Total atoms \(= 2 \times 4 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 48.2 \times 10^{23} \approx 48 \times 10^{23}\).
Matches option D.

stem: What will be the mass of 100 atoms of hydrogen?
solution:
One mole of hydrogen atoms weighs \(1\,\text{g}\) and contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.
Mass of one atom \(= \dfrac{1}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} = 1.66 \times 10^{-24}\,\text{g}\).
Mass of 100 atoms \(= 100 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-24} = 1.66 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{g}\).
Matches option B.

stem: How many atoms in total are present in 1 kg of sugar?
solution:
Sugar is \(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\), molar mass \(342\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles in \(1\,\text{kg} = \dfrac{1000}{342} = 2.924\,\text{mol}\).
Atoms per molecule \(= 12 + 22 + 11 = 45\).
Total atoms \(= 2.924 \times 45 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 7.92 \times 10^{25}\).
Matches option A.

stem: How many moles of oxygen gas can be produced during electrolytic decomposition of 180 g of water?
solution:
\(2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2\), so \(2\,\text{mol}\) of water give \(1\,\text{mol}\) of oxygen.
Moles of water \(= \dfrac{180}{18} = 10\,\text{mol}\).
Moles of \(\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{10}{2} = 5\,\text{mol}\).
Matches option B.

stem: 1.4 moles of phosphorus trichloride are present in a sample. How many atoms are there in the sample?
solution:
\(\text{PCl}_3\) holds \(1 + 3 = 4\) atoms per molecule.
Moles of atoms \(= 1.4 \times 4 = 5.6\,\text{mol}\).
Number of atoms \(= 5.6 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.372 \times 10^{24}\).
Matches option D.

stem: What will be the standard molar volume of He, if its density is \(0.1784\,\text{g}/\text{L}\) at STP?
solution:
Molar volume \(= \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{density}}\).
Helium is monatomic, molar mass \(4\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
\(V_m = \dfrac{4}{0.1784} = 22.4\,\text{L}\), the standard molar volume every gas shows at STP.
Matches option B.

stem: In a mixture of gases, the volume content of a gas is 0.06% at STP. Calculate the number of molecules of the gas in 1 L of the mixture.
solution:
By Avogadro's law the volume per cent of a gas equals its mole per cent.
Volume of the gas in \(1\,\text{L}\) of mixture \(= \dfrac{0.06}{100} \times 1 = 6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{L}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-4}}{22.4} = 2.68 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol}\).
Molecules \(= 2.68 \times 10^{-5} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.61 \times 10^{19}\).
Matches option D.

stem: Which of the following formulae is not correctly depicted?
optA: Molar mass \(= \frac{\text{Mass of substance}}{\text{Moles of substance}}\) Or \(M = \frac{W}{n}\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
optB: Number of moles of a substance \(= \frac{\text{Mass of substance}}{\text{Molar mass}}\) or \(x = \frac{w}{m}\,\text{mol}\)
optC: Number of molecules \(= \frac{\text{Mass of the substance}}{\text{Molar mass}} \times \text{Avogadro's no}\) Or no. of molecules \(= \frac{w}{M} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23}\) molecules
optD: Mole \(\times\) Molar mass = Number of molecules
solution:
Moles \(\times\) molar mass \(= \text{mol} \times \text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = \text{g}\), which is the MASS of the substance, not a count of molecules.
To reach a number of molecules the moles must be multiplied by Avogadro's number instead.
The other three relations are correct: \(M = w/n\), \(n = w/M\), and number of molecules \(= \dfrac{w}{M} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\).
Matches option D.

stem: What is the mass of carbon dioxide which contains the same number of molecules as are contained in 40 g of oxygen?
solution:
Equal numbers of molecules means equal numbers of moles.
Moles of \(\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{40}{32} = 1.25\,\text{mol}\).
Mass of \(1.25\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{CO}_2 = 1.25 \times 44 = 55\,\text{g}\).
Matches option B.

stem: What will be the weight of CO having the same number of oxygen atoms as present in 22 g of \(\text{CO}_2\)?
solution:
Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{22}{44} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\), and each molecule holds 2 oxygen atoms.
Moles of oxygen atoms \(= 0.5 \times 2 = 1\,\text{mol}\).
CO holds 1 oxygen atom per molecule, so \(1\,\text{mol}\) of CO is needed to supply the same \(1\,\text{mol}\) of oxygen atoms.
Mass \(= 1 \times 28 = 28\,\text{g}\).
Matches option A.

stem: How many number of aluminium ions are present in \(0.051\,\text{g}\) of aluminium oxide?
solution:
Molar mass of \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 = 2(27) + 3(16) = 102\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{0.051}{102} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\).
Each formula unit gives 2 aluminium ions, so moles of \(\text{Al}^{3+} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\).
Number of ions \(= 1 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{20}\).
Matches option A.

stem: How many grams of CaO are required to react with 852 g of \(\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}\)?
solution:
\(6\text{CaO} + \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} \rightarrow 2\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2\).
Molar mass of \(\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} = 4(31) + 10(16) = 284\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{852}{284} = 3\,\text{mol}\).
Moles of CaO \(= 6 \times 3 = 18\,\text{mol}\).
Mass \(= 18 \times 56 = 1008\,\text{g}\).
Matches option B.

stem: How many oxygen atoms will be present in 88 g of \(\text{CO}_2\)?
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] The correct value \(24.088 \times 10^{23}\) is printed TWICE, as two different options. A student who shades either one has answered correctly, so this question cannot be graded on a single key. The OMR must accept both.

Moles of \(\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{88}{44} = 2\,\text{mol}\).
Each molecule holds 2 oxygen atoms, so moles of oxygen atoms \(= 4\,\text{mol}\).
Number of oxygen atoms \(= 4 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 24.09 \times 10^{23}\).
The remaining values, \(44 \times 10^{23}\) and \(22 \times 10^{24}\), are an order of magnitude or more away from this.
Matches option A.
reviewNote: PRINTED DEFECT WITH A LIVE GRADING CONSEQUENCE. The correct value is 4 x 6.022e23 = 24.088e23, and the paper prints 24.08e23 at BOTH (a) and (b), character-identical (already in the transcription note). So the DUPLICATE IS THE ANSWER, not a duplicated distractor: a student who shades (b) has given the correct value and would be marked wrong against a key of (a). Recommend the OMR accept BOTH (a) and (b). The task briefing stated the correct value sits at a different option so the key is unaffected - that is not what the arithmetic gives; the only correct value is 24.08e23 and it is the duplicated one. Key recorded as the first printed occurrence.

stem: What is the total number of electrons present in \(1.6\,\text{g}\) of methane?
solution:
Moles of \(\text{CH}_4 = \dfrac{1.6}{16} = 0.1\,\text{mol}\).
Electrons per molecule \(= 6\) from carbon \(+\ 4 \times 1\) from hydrogen \(= 10\).
Moles of electrons \(= 0.1 \times 10 = 1\,\text{mol}\).
Number of electrons \(= 1 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\).
Matches option A.

stem: A person adds 1.71 gram of sugar \((\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11})\) in order to sweeten his tea. The number of carbon atoms added are: ( mol mass of sugar = 342 ).
solution:
Moles of sugar \(= \dfrac{1.71}{342} = 0.005\,\text{mol}\).
Each molecule of \(\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}\) holds 12 carbon atoms, so moles of carbon \(= 0.005 \times 12 = 0.06\,\text{mol}\).
Number of carbon atoms \(= 0.06 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.6 \times 10^{22}\).
Matches option A.

stem: 7.5 grams of a gas occupy 5.8 litres of volume at STP, the gas is:
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] No printed option is correct. The printed 5.8 L gives a molar mass of 28.97, which lies almost exactly between the two candidate gases (28 and 30). A volume of 5.6 L would give exactly 30.0, so 5.8 is very likely a misprint, but the paper cannot be graded fairly as it stands.

At STP one mole occupies \(22.4\,\text{L}\), so \(M = \dfrac{\text{mass} \times 22.4}{\text{volume}}\).
Taking the volume as \(5.6\,\text{L}\): \(M = \dfrac{7.5 \times 22.4}{5.6} = 30.0\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Molar masses of the alternatives are \(\text{NO} = 30\), \(\text{N}_2\text{O} = 44\), \(\text{CO} = 28\) and \(\text{CO}_2 = 44\).
Only nitric oxide has molar mass \(30\).
Matches option A.
reviewNote: PRINTED DEFECT - no printed option is exactly correct as the stem stands. The page reads 5.8 litres (verified at 16x), giving M = 7.5 x 22.4 / 5.8 = 28.97 g/mol, which matches none of the four. Two reconstructions exist and they point to DIFFERENT letters: 5.6 L gives exactly 30.0 = NO (a one-digit change, 8 -> 6), while 6.0 L gives exactly 28.0 = CO (a two-digit change). Judged purely by nearness to 28.97 the CO option is marginally closer (0.97 away against 1.03 for NO) - that is within noise, so nearness does not decide it. The key is recorded as NO because the one-digit correction lands on an EXACT hit, far stronger evidence of the setter's intent than a 3% difference between the two gaps. If pass 2 returns CO that is a defensible disagreement; adjudicate against the source, or drop this question from scoring.

stem:
Match the following:

| Column-I | Column-II |
|---|---|
| (A) 88 g of \(\text{CO}_2\) | (I) 0.25 mol |
| (B) \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) | (II) 2 mol |
| (C) 5.6 litres of \(\text{O}_2\) at STP | (III) 1 mol |
| (D) 96 g of \(\text{O}_2\) | (IV) \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules |
| (E) 1 mol of any gas | (V) 3 mol |
solution:
Work out each entry of Column-I.
\(88\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CO}_2 = \dfrac{88}{44} = 2\,\text{mol}\).
\(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules of \(\text{H}_2\text{O} = 1\,\text{mol}\).
\(5.6\,\text{L}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) at STP \(= \dfrac{5.6}{22.4} = 0.25\,\text{mol}\).
\(96\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{O}_2 = \dfrac{96}{32} = 3\,\text{mol}\).
1 mol of any gas contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) molecules.
So (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(V), (E)-(IV).
Matches option B.

stem: Same mass of glucose \((\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6)\) and acetic acid (\(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\)) contain
solution:
Glucose \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6\) has molar mass \(180\) and acetic acid \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\) has molar mass \(60\); both reduce to the same empirical formula \(\text{CH}_2\text{O}\), of empirical mass \(30\).
Take \(1\,\text{g}\) of each.
Carbon: \(\dfrac{6}{180} = \dfrac{1}{30}\,\text{mol}\) against \(\dfrac{2}{60} = \dfrac{1}{30}\,\text{mol}\) - equal.
Hydrogen: \(\dfrac{12}{180} = \dfrac{1}{15}\,\text{mol}\) against \(\dfrac{4}{60} = \dfrac{1}{15}\,\text{mol}\) - equal.
Oxygen: \(\dfrac{6}{180} = \dfrac{1}{30}\,\text{mol}\) against \(\dfrac{2}{60} = \dfrac{1}{30}\,\text{mol}\) - equal.
All three counts agree, because equal masses of two compounds sharing an empirical formula contain the same number of empirical units.
Matches option D.

stem: At NTP, 1.0 g hydrogen has volume in litre
solution:
Hydrogen gas is \(\text{H}_2\), molar mass \(2\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{1.0}{2} = 0.5\,\text{mol}\).
Volume at NTP \(= 0.5 \times 22.4 = 11.2\,\text{L}\).
Matches option D.

stem: The number of moles of \(\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2\) in 13.5 g is
solution:
Molar mass of \(\text{SO}_2\text{Cl}_2 = 32 + 2(16) + 2(35.5) = 32 + 32 + 71 = 135\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{13.5}{135} = 0.1\,\text{mol}\).
Matches option A.

stem: Ratio of number of oxygen atoms in \(\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2\) and \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\), if both contain same number of P atoms, is
solution:
Compare the two formulae on a per-phosphorus basis.
\(\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2\) holds 2 P and \(2 \times 4 = 8\) O, i.e. \(\dfrac{8}{2} = 4\) oxygen atoms per phosphorus atom.
\(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3\) holds 1 P and 3 O, i.e. 3 oxygen atoms per phosphorus atom.
For the same number of phosphorus atoms the oxygen atoms stand in the ratio \(4 : 3\).
Matches option B.

stem: Cortisone is a molecular substance containing 21 atoms of carbon per molecule. The mass percentage of carbon in cortisone is 69.98%. Its molar mass is:
solution:
Each molecule holds 21 carbon atoms, so one mole holds \(21 \times 12 = 252\,\text{g}\) of carbon.
That carbon is \(69.98\%\) of the molar mass, so \(0.6998\,M = 252\).
\(M = \dfrac{252}{0.6998} = 360.1\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Matches option D.

stem: If 1.5 moles of oxygen combine with Al to form \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\), the weight of Al used in the reaction is:
solution:
\(4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\), so aluminium and oxygen react in the ratio \(4 : 3\).
Moles of Al \(= \dfrac{4}{3} \times 1.5 = 2\,\text{mol}\).
Mass of Al \(= 2 \times 27 = 54\,\text{g}\).
As a check, \(1.5\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{O}_2\) is \(3\,\text{mol}\) of oxygen atoms, which builds \(1\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3\) and so needs \(2\,\text{mol}\) of aluminium.
Matches option C.

stem: When 100 g of ethylene polymerises entirely to polyethene, the weight of polyethene formed as per the equation \(n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4) \rightarrow (-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-)_n\) is:
solution:
Addition polymerisation joins the monomer units with nothing added and nothing eliminated, so the repeating unit \((-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-)\) has exactly the same formula mass as the monomer \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\).
Mass is conserved, so all \(100\,\text{g}\) of ethylene becomes \(100\,\text{g}\) of polyethene, whatever the value of \(n\).
An answer carrying \(n\) would mean the mass depended on the chain length, which it does not.
Matches option B.

stem: The mass of 70% \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) required for neutralization of 1 mol of NaOH.
solution:
\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\), so \(1\,\text{mol}\) of NaOH needs \(0.5\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\).
Mass of pure \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 0.5 \times 98 = 49\,\text{g}\).
The sample is only \(70\%\) acid, so mass of sample \(= \dfrac{49}{0.70} = 70\,\text{g}\).
Matches option C.

subtopic: Balancing Redox Reactions and Oxidized/Reduced Species
stem: For the redox reaction \(\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), the correct whole number stoichiometric coefficients of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\), \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\) and \(\text{H}^+\) are respectively:
solution:
Manganese falls from \(+7\) in \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) to \(+2\), gaining 5 electrons.
Carbon rises from \(+3\) in \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\) to \(+4\) in \(\text{CO}_2\), and each oxalate carries 2 carbons, so it loses 2 electrons.
Electron balance: \(2 \times 5 = 10 = 5 \times 2\), i.e. 2 permanganate to 5 oxalate.
\(2\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + 16\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}\).
Check: oxygen is \(8 + 20 = 28\) on the left and \(20 + 8 = 28\) on the right; charge is \(-2 - 10 + 16 = +4\) on both sides.
The coefficients asked for are \(2, 5, 16\).
Matches option A.

subtopic: Balancing Redox Reactions and Oxidized/Reduced Species
stem: In the reaction \(\text{X}^- + \text{XO}_3^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{X}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\), the molar ratio in which \(\text{X}^-\) and \(\text{XO}_3^-\) react is:
solution:
\(\text{X}^-\) is oxidised from \(-1\) to \(0\) in \(\text{X}_2\), losing 1 electron per atom.
\(\text{XO}_3^-\) is reduced from \(+5\) to \(0\), gaining 5 electrons per atom.
Balancing electrons needs 5 atoms of \(\text{X}^-\) for every 1 of \(\text{XO}_3^-\), so the molar ratio is \(5 : 1\).
The full equation \(5\text{X}^- + \text{XO}_3^- + 6\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 3\text{X}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}\) balances in X (6 each side), O (3 each side), H (6 each side) and charge (0 each side).
Matches option B.

subtopic: Balancing Redox Reactions and Oxidized/Reduced Species
stem: \(\text{CN}^-\) is oxidized by \(\text{NO}_3^-\) in presence of acid: \(a\text{CN}^- + b\text{NO}_3^- + c\text{H}^+ \rightarrow (a+b)\,\text{NO} + a\text{CO}_2 + \frac{c}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}\) What are the whole number values of a, b, c in that order:
solution:
Assign oxidation numbers. In \(\text{CN}^-\), carbon is \(+2\) and nitrogen \(-3\); these become \(+4\) in \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(+2\) in NO, so each \(\text{CN}^-\) loses \(2 + 5 = 7\) electrons.
In \(\text{NO}_3^-\), nitrogen falls from \(+5\) to \(+2\), gaining 3 electrons.
Electron balance: \(7a = 3b\), so \(a : b = 3 : 7\), giving \(a = 3\) and \(b = 7\).
Charge balance: \(-a - b + c = 0\), so \(c = a + b = 10\).
Check oxygen: left \(= 3b = 21\); right \(= (a+b) + 2a + \dfrac{c}{2} = 10 + 6 + 5 = 21\).
So \(a, b, c = 3, 7, 10\); each of the other three sets fails both the charge balance and the oxygen balance.
Matches option D.

stem: 36.5 % HCl has density equal to \(1.20\,\text{g}\,\text{mL}^{-1}\). The molarity (M) and molality (m), respectively, are
solution:
Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of solution, which holds \(36.5\,\text{g}\) of HCl, i.e. \(\dfrac{36.5}{36.5} = 1\,\text{mol}\).
Volume of that solution \(= \dfrac{100}{1.20} = 83.33\,\text{mL} = 0.08333\,\text{L}\).
Molarity \(= \dfrac{1}{0.08333} = 12\,\text{M}\).
Mass of solvent \(= 100 - 36.5 = 63.5\,\text{g} = 0.0635\,\text{kg}\).
Molality \(= \dfrac{1}{0.0635} = 15.7\,\text{m}\).
Matches option D.

stem: An aqueous solution of ethanol has density 1.025 g/mL and it is 2M. What is the molality of this solution?
solution:
Take \(1\,\text{L}\) of solution.
Mass of solution \(= 1000 \times 1.025 = 1025\,\text{g}\).
It holds \(2\,\text{mol}\) of ethanol, mass \(= 2 \times 46 = 92\,\text{g}\).
Mass of water \(= 1025 - 92 = 933\,\text{g} = 0.933\,\text{kg}\).
Molality \(= \dfrac{2}{0.933} = 2.143\,\text{m}\).
Matches option B.

stem: Mole fraction of ethyl alcohol in aqueous ethyl alcohol \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})\) solution is 0.25. Hence percentage of ethyl alcohol by weight is:
solution:
Take \(1\,\text{mol}\) of solution in total: \(0.25\,\text{mol}\) of ethanol and \(0.75\,\text{mol}\) of water.
Mass of ethanol \(= 0.25 \times 46 = 11.5\,\text{g}\).
Mass of water \(= 0.75 \times 18 = 13.5\,\text{g}\).
Total mass \(= 25\,\text{g}\).
Per cent by weight \(= \dfrac{11.5}{25} \times 100 = 46\%\).
Matches option D.

stem: Calculate the mass percent (w/w) of sulphuric acid in a solution prepared by dissolving 4 g of sulphur trioxide in a 100 ml sulphuric acid solution containing 80 mass percent (w/w) of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) and having a density of 1.96 g/ml. (molecular weight of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) = 98). Take reaction \(\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)
solution:
Mass of the original solution \(= 100 \times 1.96 = 196\,\text{g}\).
\(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) already present \(= 0.80 \times 196 = 156.8\,\text{g}\).
Moles of \(\text{SO}_3\) added \(= \dfrac{4}{80} = 0.05\,\text{mol}\); by \(\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) this makes \(0.05 \times 98 = 4.9\,\text{g}\) more acid.
Total \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 = 156.8 + 4.9 = 161.7\,\text{g}\); the water consumed stays inside the solution, so the total mass is simply \(196 + 4 = 200\,\text{g}\).
Mass per cent \(= \dfrac{161.7}{200} \times 100 = 80.85\%\).
Matches option A.
reviewNote: The exact value is 80.85%, and the nearest printed option reads 80.8% - a rounding of it (80.85 truncates to 80.8 and rounds half-up to 80.9). Flagged only because 'None of these' is on the paper, so a strict reader could argue for that instead; the 0.05 percentage-point gap is a print rounding rather than a different answer, so the key is recorded as 80.8%.

stem: The sodium salt of methyl orange has 7% sodium. What is the minimum molecular weight of the compound?
solution:
A minimum molecular weight follows from assuming the smallest whole number of the element - here one sodium atom per molecule.
That atom contributes \(23\,\text{g}\) per mole and is \(7\%\) of the molar mass.
\(0.07\,M = 23\), so \(M = \dfrac{23}{0.07} = 328.57\).
Matches option C.

stem: 112.0 mL of \(\text{NO}_2\) at STP was liquefied, the density of the liquid being \(1.15\,\text{g}\,\text{mL}^{-1}\). Calculate the volume and the number of molecules in the liquid \(\text{NO}_2\).
solution:
Moles of \(\text{NO}_2 = \dfrac{112.0}{22400} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\).
Molar mass of \(\text{NO}_2 = 14 + 32 = 46\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), so mass \(= 5 \times 10^{-3} \times 46 = 0.23\,\text{g}\).
Volume of the liquid \(= \dfrac{0.23}{1.15} = 0.20\,\text{mL}\).
Number of molecules \(= 5 \times 10^{-3} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.01 \times 10^{21}\).
Matches option B.

stem: Common salt obtained from sea - water contains 96% NaCl by mass. The approximate number of molecules of NaCl present in 10.0 g of the common salt is: (At. wt. Na = 23)
solution:
Mass of NaCl \(= 0.96 \times 10.0 = 9.6\,\text{g}\).
Molar mass of NaCl \(= 23 + 35.5 = 58.5\,\text{g}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
Moles \(= \dfrac{9.6}{58.5} = 0.164\,\text{mol}\).
Number of formula units \(= 0.164 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 9.88 \times 10^{22} \approx 10^{23}\).
Matches option C.
